sections.h2: What makes selling a house in Cicero different from selling in other Illinois towns?
sections.html:
Cicero requires two local steps on nearly every home sale: Real Estate Transfer Stamps and a Certificate of Compliance. The Town's Building Department explains both on its "Buying Or Selling A Home?" page, and they affect how fast a sale can close and who ends up paying for repairs.

Cicero is a town of about 5.87 square miles in Cook County, in the Chicago area. The Census Bureau estimated 81,858 residents on July 1, 2025, down 4.0 percent from the April 2020 base of 85,294. The 2020 count works out to 14,538 people per square mile.

A seller here usually has three paths: fix everything the Town flags and sell with a certificate in hand, sell as-is and let the buyer take on the compliance work, or complete a transfer that the Town classes as exempt. Each is described below with the paperwork it needs.

sections.h2: How does the Cicero Certificate of Compliance work?
sections.html:
A Town building inspector walks the property, hands the owner a list of everything out of line with the Town Code, and the property must meet that list before a certificate is issued. The Town describes the steps as an inspection, a compliance checklist and then bringing the property up to code.

The Town treats a "transfer" broadly. It covers a deed, articles of agreement for a deed, an assignment of the beneficial interest in a land trust, using real property as loan collateral and adding a present beneficiary to a land trust. Purchasing transfer stamps is mandatory for all transfers, including those that are otherwise exempt from the compliance step.

The three ways to transfer a home in Cicero
RouteWho handles complianceWhat the Town says
Sale with a current certificateSeller, before the saleThe property already meets Town Code, so the transfer is straightforward for the buyer
As-is saleBuyer, after the purchaseThe buyer assumes responsibility for bringing the property into compliance and obtaining the certificate
Exempt transactionNo certificate neededApplies to categories such as court-ordered or familial transfers and vacant land

Source: Town of Cicero Building Department. The Town advises owners to consult its compliance staff throughout the process and to allow ample time, because the review covers multiple parts of the property.

sections.h2: Which Cicero transfers are exempt from the compliance step?
sections.html:
The Town lists four exempt categories, and for those no inspection or certificate is required. Transfer stamps are still required for every one of them.

  • Court-ordered transfers: tax deeds, sheriff's deeds and transfers made under orders of local, county, state or federal courts.
  • Vacant land: transactions involving only vacant land.
  • No change in ownership interest: transfers that do not give a new party an ownership or beneficial interest.
  • Familial transfers: adding a spouse to a deed under Section 22-281 of the Town's Code of Ordinances, in effect since March 24, 2017.

If you inherited a Cicero home and are unsure which category applies, ask the Building Department before you list. The Town Hall is at 4949 West Cermak Road, open Monday through Friday from 8 AM to 6 PM, and the main line is (708) 656-3600.

sections.h2: What does the state and county paperwork look like for a Cicero sale?
sections.html:
Cicero deeds are recorded by the Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division, and the state transfer tax is 50 cents for each $500 of value or fraction of $500 stated in the declaration. That rate is set in 35 ILCS 200/31-10.

The Clerk's office records and maintains land records, lets the public search them by property index number or party name, and runs a Property Fraud Unit that helps owners investigate suspicious filings against their property. It is open 9 am to 5 pm and takes its last customer at 4:45 pm. The Town's page does not print a stamp amount, so ask the Building Department what the stamps cost and ask your title company which other charges appear on the closing statement.

On the disclosure side, Illinois law requires the seller of residential property to complete a report and give it to the buyer before the contract is signed. Section 20 of the Residential Real Property Disclosure Act sets that rule, and the report asks about basement leakage, roof and foundation defects, radon, lead paint and lead pipes, among other items. A house that needs work can still be sold in as-is condition, but the questions still have to be answered honestly.

sections.h2: What does the Cicero housing market look like in Census data?
sections.html:
Cicero is a town of renters and owners in nearly equal measure, and its homes are family-sized. Census Bureau figures for 2020 to 2024 put owner occupancy at 54.6 percent, the median value of an owner-occupied unit at $249,400 and median gross rent at $1,154.

The same tables count 24,432 households averaging 3.36 people, higher than in Chicago, Crystal Lake or Danville. Median household income is $70,842, 95.0 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, and 79.8 percent speak a language other than English at home. Hispanic or Latino residents are 87.5 percent of the population and 40.6 percent of residents are foreign-born.

Those numbers describe a long-tenured community with large households, which is the group most likely to be shopping for a family-sized house.

sections.h2: How did Cicero get its shape, schools and transit?
sections.html:
Cicero was incorporated on February 28, 1867, and it once covered far more ground. The original Cicero Township was about six times the size of today's town, until Oak Park and Berwyn were carved out and areas such as Austin were annexed by Chicago. The old Hawthorne Works factory employed more than 40,000 people at its peak, and the area long had a Czech and Bohemian character along what was then 22nd Street, now Cermak Road.

Cicero Elementary School District 99 operates 16 schools, which makes it one of the largest districts outside Chicago. High school students attend schools in J. Sterling Morton High School District 201, and Morton College is in town. Two private Catholic schools serve grades pre-K through 8.

For commuters, Cicero sits on two freight rail lines, the BNSF Railway and the Belt Railway of Chicago. The Metra BNSF Line stops near Cicero Avenue and 26th Street, the CTA Pink Line runs from its 54th/Cermak terminal to the Loop, and several Pace and CTA bus routes cross town.

sections.h2: Which Cook County tax items should a Cicero seller check?
sections.html:
Check whether the house has the Homeowner Exemption on its tax bill before closing. The Cook County Assessor says the exemption cuts the equalized assessed value by $10,000, renews automatically once granted, and requires that you own and live in the home as your principal residence.

  • Seniors 65 or older may also qualify for the Senior Exemption.
  • The Senior Freeze has an income limit of $65,000 or less for calendar year 2024 and must be filed each year.
  • Missing exemptions for tax years 2021 through 2025 can be redeemed with a Certificate of Error.

Taxes in Illinois are billed in installments, and the second installment bill shows the exemptions that were applied. At the closing table, ask the title company to show how the current year's bill is split between you and the buyer, and whether any installment is still unpaid.

sections.h2: What costs should a Cicero seller weigh in a cash offer?
sections.html:
The main question is whether a buyer who takes the house as-is leaves you with more or less than repairing it for the Town and listing it. A compliance checklist can include items you would never fix for your own use, so get the inspection list first, price the work with a contractor, and then compare it with the cash number.

  • Total of the repair bids needed to earn a certificate.
  • Months of mortgage, utility and tax payments while the house is listed.
  • Who buys the transfer stamps and who pays for the compliance inspection.
  • Whether the contract states plainly that the buyer will obtain the certificate after closing.

Put every figure side by side before deciding. A quick, certain closing is worth something, but only you can say how much.

faqs.q: Do I need a Certificate of Compliance to sell my Cicero house?
faqs.a: Usually yes, unless the transfer is exempt. The Town lets you sell with a current certificate or sell as-is, in which case the buyer takes on the work of obtaining it after the purchase.

faqs.q: Are transfer stamps required for every Cicero sale?
faqs.a: Yes. The Town says Real Estate Transfer Stamps are required for all real estate transfers, even those that are exempt from the compliance step.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Cicero house with code violations?
faqs.a: Yes, through an as-is sale. The buyer assumes responsibility for bringing the property into compliance, so the price usually reflects what the Town's checklist would require.

faqs.q: Who records the deed for a Cicero home?
faqs.a: The Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division records it. Your title company or attorney normally files the deed along with the state transfer declaration.

faqs.q: Is adding my spouse to the deed treated as a sale in Cicero?
faqs.a: It counts as a transfer, but the Town lists adding a spouse to a deed under Section 22-281 as an exempt familial transfer. No inspection or certificate is required, though the transfer stamps are.
